definition: A standard contract clause, from the French for 'greater force,' that releases both parties from liability when extraordinary, uncontrollable events (war, natural disaster, etc.) prevent performance.
core_idea: Force majeure protects both counterparties from breach liability when performance becomes impossible due to events outside either party's control.
key_points: Covers events like wars and natural disasters that are outside the control of either contracting party.
Its effect is to excuse one or both parties from fulfilling contract obligations under such circumstances.
relationships: Relevant to firm contracts, where nonperformance otherwise carries legal recourse.
trading_implications: Even firm, legally binding contracts carry an escape valve for extraordinary disruptions, which matters when assessing counterparty delivery risk.
